rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Truth’ denotes the Qur’an and its true religion, while ‘evil’ denotes the false religion the Qur’an came to obliterate.
rows.anchor: refers to the Qur’ ān and the religion of truth brought by it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The migration instruction is followed by a proclamation of truth’s victory because a messenger’s migration prefigures the call’s success and the opponents’ defeat.
rows.anchor: the migration of a messenger of God is in reality a prelude to the success of his call

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Evil has no root in human nature and spreads like weeds when left uncleared; once removed, truth flourishes because human nature is fitted to it.
rows.anchor: evil has no basis in human nature. Like self-growing weeds and bushes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophecy was fulfilled at the conquest of Makkah, when the Prophet broke the Ka‘bah’s idols with his spear while reciting the verse.
rows.anchor: At the conquest of Makkah, this prophecy was fulfilled

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is wholly a cure and mercy for believers, but increases the unjust in loss because denial after truth is clear makes them deserve punishment in both lives.
rows.anchor: whatever the Almighty has revealed in it is an antidote to their spiritual and intellectual ailments

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although ‘human being’ is general, context identifies the Quraysh miscreants who arrogantly evaded God’s Book and Messenger.
rows.anchor: Almighty referred to them by a general word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about turning aside intensifies evasion: polite evasion is possible, but hatred makes a person physically turn away too.
rows.anchor: when a person evades something because of hate and dislike, he physically turns away too

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People should show gratitude in ease and patience in trials; instead, blessings make the opponents arrogant enough to demand punishment, and any seizure would come too late.
rows.anchor: favours have made them arrogant to such an extent that they demand a sign of punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though indefinite in form, the word ‘each’ functions as definite here and refers to the groups or people mentioned earlier.
rows.anchor: in certain instances as is the case here, it becomes a definite noun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Way’ means path: opponents may follow their own course while the Prophet maintains his; unfolding circumstances will show who reaches the destination.
rows.anchor: The implication is that if these people are not willing to listen to the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse expresses the Prophet’s trust in God: he should consign his opponents’ affair to God and remain firm on his position.
rows.anchor: He is directed to consign their matter to God and strictly adhere to his view

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing section answers opponents’ objections and demands for signs, while reassuring the Prophet that knowledgeable people believe and sign-demanders will not.
rows.anchor: those objections of the opponents of the Prophet (sws) are responded to

none: Arabic verse text only; no commentary point.
Translation of verses only; no commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here rūḥ means divine revelation, the life of the heart and intellect as spirit is life for the body; the Qur’an also calls revelation rūḥ in 16:2, 40:15, and 42:52.
rows.anchor: the life of our heart and intellect is divine revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus similarly taught that human life depends on every word from God, not bread alone.
rows.anchor: Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers’ question about the spirit was ridicule rather than sincere inquiry; only one who experiences it understands, and they need not be told every divine secret.
rows.anchor: their question was not an actual inquiry: it was to ridicule and make fun of it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their concealed question was why revelation did not come to them; the cited language says God chooses particular servants, since not everyone is worthy, and its reality is known only to God.
rows.anchor: In other words, not every person is worthy of this

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revelation is wholly governed by God: the Prophet neither acquires it at will nor can refuse or retain it if God removes it; it is a divine bounty.
rows.anchor: he does not even have the power to keep it with him if God wanted to take it away

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since even the Prophet cannot produce revelation by his own intent, humanity and jinn together cannot produce a Qur’an like it; the author says history shows failed imitators became objects of ridicule.
rows.anchor: Even if mankind and jinnkind collaborate in this matter, they will never succeed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relevant verb means presenting something in different styles; ḥikam means words of wisdom and sagacity, a familiar Arabic usage.
rows.anchor: mention something in different styles and multiple ways

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author cites the Ḥamāsī poet’s line as an example of wise sayings directed to sensible people.
rows.anchor: O Badr! A wise person states words of wisdom for the sensible only

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the miraculous Qur’an presents wisdom in many forms, opponents have no excuse that guidance failed to reach them; persistent denial is their own wretchedness.
rows.anchor: The Book of God has conclusively communicated the truth to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When īmān takes the preposition ل here, it means acknowledging something, not accepting faith; the opponents make miraculous displays conditions for acknowledging prophethood.
rows.anchor: it only means to acknowledge something

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet answers that he never claimed divinity; God is exalted above partners, and as a human messenger his duty is to deliver, not perform their demands.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) is only a human being and His messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s guidance has already reached them clearly with arguments and rationale; objecting that a human was sent as messenger is a feeble excuse born of arrogance.
rows.anchor: it has come before them in a very clear form with incontestable proofs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A messenger must be of the same species as the addressees so he can serve as their exemplar; an angel cannot fill that role for humans.
rows.anchor: a messenger has to belong to the same species as his addressees

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels walking on earth would be there only to execute God’s intent and command, not as its permanent residents.
rows.anchor: They are not permanent residents here

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After truth is conclusively delivered, God’s witness suffices: opponents reject from arrogance rather than lack of evidence, and God will judge whether they recognized the prophethood yet refused.
rows.anchor: it is not the lack of arguments which is not making them accept faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s guidance comes to people who use sight for His signs, speech to bear witness, and hearing for His words; those who deliberately render these faculties blind, deaf, and dumb do not receive it.
rows.anchor: their ears to hear the words of God and his Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents, having misused their faculties, merit being dragged face-first, blind, deaf, and dumb into Hell; 54:48 likewise depicts them dragged into the flames.
rows.anchor: Faces which were blessed with the faculties of sight, hearing and speech

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their punishment follows denial despite seeing God’s signs and reviving the dead, while insisting resurrection is impossible; God will demonstrate its possibility.
rows.anchor: in spite of observing the signs of God’s power and of raising the dead to life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The One who created heaven and earth can recreate people; resurrection has an appointed time, so they should not demand its haste.
rows.anchor: Is recreating the heavens and the earth more difficult than creating them again?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The miserly verse addresses Quraysh leaders’ arrogance: despite worldly favors, they resented prophethood being given to a poor person rather than themselves.
rows.anchor: It has been pointed out earlier that

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day of Judgement has a fixed time, so opponents should not demand that it arrive hastily.
rows.anchor: The time of the Day of Judgement is fixed. They should not show haste in its arrival

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ nine miracles answer Quraysh’s demands: signs do not secure faith, since Pharaoh called Moses mad despite them; the Prophet is assured his audience would react similarly.
rows.anchor: Moses (sws) was equipped with nine miracles but the Pharaoh regarded him to be a mad man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to ask the Israelites insinuates that they had joined the anti-Islam campaign and urged Quraysh to demand miracles; their own response to Moses’ signs ended in drowning.
rows.anchor: by that time, the Israelites had fully become part of the campaign against Islam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the opponents were punished, God settled the Israelites in the land He had promised them, the holy land, and reminded them of the Hereafter promise they later forgot.
rows.anchor: once their opponents had been punished

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After addressing related issues, the discourse returns to its opening theme of revelation and the Qur’an’s purity and truth; the Prophet’s role is to warn and give good news.
rows.anchor: Once they finished, the original topic is once again reverted to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an was revealed in portions so the Prophet could recite it gradually for people to absorb; this staging serves creatures’ needs and circumstances.
rows.anchor: The reason for its revelation in parts is because he can gradually recite it out to his people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Those given knowledge’ are the righteous among the People of the Book, who were awaiting a messenger and book according to their scriptures and recognized the Qur’an as fulfillment of prophecy.
rows.anchor: refers to the righteous among the People of the Book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This righteous group prostrated when the Qur’an was recited, thanked God for fulfilling His promise, and wept with humility.
rows.anchor: they would fall down in prostration and would wholeheartedly thank God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allāh and Raḥmān were both used as names of God among Arabs, and Raḥmān may have been more popular with the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: the Arabs would use both

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh alleged that People of the Book helped the Prophet prepare the Qur’an, invoking the name Raḥmān as evidence; the author links this earlier accusation to 25:4.
rows.anchor: They posited that some among the people of the Book help the Prophet (sws) in preparing this Book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents inferred from the name Raḥmān that the Prophet was trying to impose the People of the Book’s traditions and religion.
rows.anchor: this person was trying to impose on them the traditions and religion of the People of the Book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an answers that objection: bias toward a name should not prevent acceptance of truth, since God may be called by any name fitting His majesty.
rows.anchor: bias towards a name should not be a cause of accepting the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an rejects bias against a divine name: God has several names, and any name befitting His majesty may be used.
rows.anchor: God has several names and He can be called by every name that befits His majesty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author suggests idolaters may have objected to Muslim prayer because their worship featured noise, clapping, and whistling, while Islamic prayer was solemn and dignified.
rows.anchor: In their religion, making noise, clapping and whistling had a special status in worship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to keep prayer and supplication at a moderate volume; this reflects the moderation expected of the Muslim community.
rows.anchor: since Muslims are a middle ummah, their prayers and supplications too should have moderation in them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the surah’s close the Prophet must proclaim God’s sole sovereignty: one who faces no helplessness has no need of helpers, and God is to be exalted regardless of idolaters’ conduct.
rows.anchor: How can the God Whose majesty and splendour is beyond any such state need helpers
